extraction_notes.note: One sentence both introduces $\#c(g)$ and states the Möbius-inversion count of exact-symmetry tilings; kept as one definition node since the sentence cannot be split.

Each symmetry-class paragraph identifies $\#c\langle g\rangle$ with a Stanley class/OEIS sequence and quotes a cited product formula; typed as external theorems rather than equations or paper claims, since the formulas are attributed by \cite.

The re-indexing ('inflation') of the cited formulas is the paper's own adjustment; the identification sentences of the $\langle fr\rangle$ paragraph went into the vanishing claim ClP4, while for $\langle r\rangle$ the whole paragraph is TP6.

The two TikZ figures (pairing of triangles along axes) carry only illustration of the parity arguments; captions not made nodes. The intro sentence that product formulas were proven for each symmetry class is background with no specific statement.
The note has no sections and no theorem environments although lemma/theorem/observation are declared; every node is prose, so section fields are empty.

nodes.statement: The symmetry group of the hexagon is the dihedral group of order 12, D_12, which has the presentation langle f, r mid f^2 = r^6 = (fr)^2 = erangle where, for our geometric purposes, f (for ``flip'') represents a reflection around a diameter and r (for ``rotation'') represents a rotation by 60^circ.

nodes.statement: If we denote the number of tilings which have at least the symmetries of g le langle f, rrangle by \#c(g) then the number of tilings having exactly the symmetries of g is given by the M\"obius function of the incidence algebra of this poset: sum_h le langle f, rrangle mu(g, h) \#c(h).

nodes.statement: The axis of symmetry bisects 2n triangles, which must pair up along the axis because otherwise they would be forced to pair with two triangles to maintain the symmetry. But the pairs start at the centre of the hexagon, so if n is odd there are two triangles on opposite edges which can't be paired. (See figure 1).

nodes.statement: If we divide the hexagon into six large triangles by drawing the diameters through its vertices, each of these large triangles has fracn(n+1)2 small triangles in one orientation and frac(n-1)n2 small triangles in another orientation. For langle r^3rangle we can consider a half-hexagon formed from three of the large triangles: the symmetry will give us the tiling of the other half. This half-hexagon has a surplus of n triangles in one orientation; therefore there must be n triangles along the diameter which pair across into the other half-hexagon. (See figure 2). By the rotational symmetry, these n triangles must be paired up, but if n is odd this is impossible. For even n we have \#clangle r^3rangle(2m) = \#clangle erangle(m)^2 .
nodes.raw_latex: If we divide the hexagon into six large triangles by drawing the diameters through its vertices, each of these large triangles has $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ small triangles in one orientation and $\frac{(n-1)n}{2}$ small triangles in another orientation. For $\langle r^3\rangle$ we can consider a half-hexagon formed from three of the large triangles: the symmetry will give us the tiling of the other half. This half-hexagon has a surplus of $n$ triangles in one orientation; therefore there must be $n$ triangles along the diameter which pair across into the other half-hexagon. (See figure 2). By the rotational symmetry, these $n$ triangles must be paired up, but if $n$ is odd this is impossible. For even $n$ we have $\#c\langle r^3\rangle(2m) = \#c\langle e\rangle(m)^2$ \cite{Stanley86}.
